speaker: Boaz Weinstein
title: Boaz Weinstein on the Money Stuff Podcast
question: In private credit funds, why is buying a levered fund at a 30% to 35% discount to reported NAV much less of a bargain than the headline discount implies?
guest: Some funds are very levered—some are 0.75x levered, some are 1.5x levered. That means leverage on top of a dollar of stuff for the dollar that was given. So let's just say it was a turn of leverage. If you buy something at minus 30%, it is like you are buying each loan 15 points below, not 30 points below. But then you have the fees, and some of them earn fees on what is distributed, so even with all these price declines they can still earn fees. Some have high-water marks that don't have catch-ups, some do, but there is the management fee that comes out of it. I think it is safe to say we don't think there is a lot of manager alpha these days in that space, so those fees are going to eat away at it. And on top of it, you have a NAV that everyone knows is too high. The marks are falling as we speak. So if you have NAVs that are too high across the board, you also have to take that out of the discount—you start with 15, after fees it is 13, and then you have the markdown.

points.core: Fund-level leverage shrinks the effective discount on the underlying gross loan assets.
points.note: Accept: measuring the discount against gross asset value (GAV) rather than equity NAV, e.g., at 1x leverage a 30% NAV discount equals only a 15% discount on each underlying loan. Do not credit: generic warnings that leverage increases risk.

points.core: Ongoing management fees erode the remaining discount without delivering offsetting manager alpha.
points.note: Accept: recurring management fees or distribution-linked fees continuing despite share price declines and eating into the entry discount. Do not credit: generic complaints that alternative funds charge high fees.

points.core: Stale reported NAV marks must be deducted from the apparent headline discount.
points.note: Accept: private credit marks lagging market reality or sitting overstated, meaning true economic asset value is lower than stated book NAV. Do not credit: vague skepticism about private markets without linking to mark adjustments.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The discount applies to the fund's equity, not to its underlying loans, and leverage shrinks the discount dramatically once you translate it to the asset level.

Take a fund with $100 of NAV and 1x debt-to-equity: it holds $200 of loans funded by $100 of debt. Buying the equity at a 30–35% discount means paying $65–70, so you are effectively valuing the loans at $165–170 out of $200. That is only about a 15–17.5% discount on the assets, and less still at higher leverage. The debt must be repaid at par, so every dollar of asset loss falls entirely on the equity.

That implied asset markdown is a thin cushion, for several reasons. Reported NAV rests on manager-set, often stale Level 3 marks, so true values may already be lower. Modest further credit losses or spread widening, magnified by leverage, can erase the apparent margin of safety. Falling asset values can also breach leverage covenants or asset-coverage tests, forcing sales at depressed prices or dividend cuts. Finally, management and incentive fees are typically charged on gross assets, so they consume a disproportionate share of equity returns.

points.why: The 1x leverage example correctly translates a 30–35% equity NAV discount into a 15–17.5% discount on gross loan assets.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Buying a levered private credit fund at a 30% to 35% discount to reported NAV yields a far smaller discount on the underlying loans because fund-level debt must still be repaid at par. In a 1:1 levered fund—$200 of loans backed by $100 of debt and $100 of equity NAV—paying $65 to $70 for the equity means paying $165 to $170 for $200 of assets, an effective look-through portfolio discount of only 15% to 17.5% (and even less at higher leverage). Because credit has capped par upside while fund equity absorbs first losses, portfolio write-downs of just 10% to 15% wipe out nearly that entire cushion. Moreover, reported NAVs rely on lagged, manager-estimated marks—often flattered by payment-in-kind amendments or covenant relief—rather than true market-clearing prices. Finally, management fees billed on gross assets or reported NAV magnify the fee drag on your discounted purchase price, while redemption gates, lockups, and senior credit covenants prevent quick exits at par and can trap cash under stress.

noweb.answer: A 30% to 35% discount to equity NAV shrinks dramatically once you account for fund-level leverage, stale valuations, and fee drag. Because the fund's own debt remains fixed at par, the implied discount on the underlying loans is far smaller: at a typical one-to-one debt-to-equity ratio, a 30% equity discount equates to just a 15% discount on gross assets, meaning relatively modest portfolio losses wipe out the entire cushion. Furthermore, reported NAV in private credit relies on smoothed, model-based marks for illiquid loans rather than market prices, often masking deteriorating credit quality, spread widening, and payment-in-kind amendments that keep troubled borrowers marked near par. Compounding both issues, managers typically charge base fees on gross assets or reported NAV rather than discounted market value, alongside asymmetric incentive fees on income even as principal erodes. Without a mechanism to force liquidation at NAV, the headline discount mostly prices in unrecorded credit losses and capitalized fee drag rather than offering a true margin of safety.

models.answer:
The discount applies to the fund's equity, not to its loan portfolio, and leverage magnifies small changes in asset value into large changes in NAV. Take a fund with $200 of loans financed by $100 of debt and $100 of equity. Paying 65 cents on the dollar means paying $65 for that $100 of NAV. The lenders still get their full $100 first, so you are really buying $200 of loans for $165, which is only about a 17.5% discount on the assets.

The same leverage works against you on markdowns. If the loans' reported marks are 10% too high, which is plausible given stale Level 3 valuations, rising PIK income, quietly amended loans and loans that should be non-accrual, true NAV falls by 20%. A 15–17% markdown would wipe out the 30–35% discount entirely.

The discount also has to cover management and incentive fees, the cost of the debt, years of illiquidity and the chance of forced deleveraging. Taken together, the large headline discount often just prices realistic losses rather than offering free value.

That much smaller asset-level cushion can vanish quickly because private credit valuations are illiquid, infrequent, and slow to reflect credit stress, especially when troubled borrowers use payment-in-kind interest or restructurings to avoid formal defaults. models.answer:
The 30% to 35% discount applies to the fund’s equity NAV, the amount left after subtracting debt. The fund still owes its lenders in full, so the discount buys a much smaller cushion against losses on the underlying loans.

Suppose the fund reports $100 of loans and owes $50. Its NAV is $50, and a buyer at a 30% to 35% discount pays $32.50 to $35. Including the $50 of debt, that price implies a loan portfolio value of $82.50 to $85, only 15% to 17.5% below reported marks. If the loans are worth that much less, the entire apparent bargain disappears.

Private loans trade infrequently, so reported marks can lag deteriorating credit. And if losses force the fund to sell loans to pay down debt, investors may have less time to wait for recoveries.
